chunks: Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah narrated from his father, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Hariz, from Murazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The prostration of gratitude is obligatory upon every Muslim, by which you complete your prayer and please your Lord, and the angels are amazed at you. Indeed, when the servant prays and then prostrates a prostration of gratitude, the Lord (Exalted) opens the veil between the servant and the angels, and He says, 'O My angels, look at My servant who has fulfilled My closeness (worship) and completed My covenant, then prostrated to Me in gratitude for what I bestowed upon him.' O My angels, what is his reward?' They say, 'O our Lord, Your mercy.' Then the Lord (Exalted) says, 'Then what is his reward?' They say, 'O our Lord, Your Paradise.' The Lord (Exalted) says, 'Then what?' They say, 'O our Lord, sufficiency for his need.' The Lord says, 'Then what?' So nothing of goodness remains but that the angels say it. The Lord (Exalted) says, 'O My angels, then what?' The angels say, 'O our Lord, we have no knowledge.' The Lord (Exalted) says, 'I will surely show gratitude to him as he showed gratitude to Me, and I will turn to him with My bounty and show him My mercy.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling and spiritual significance of the prostration of gratitude in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elevates Sajdat al-Shukr from a recommended act to an obligatory one, emphasizing its role in perfecting prayer and eliciting angelic wonder. The narrative illustrates the concept of *Muzahama* (divine reciprocity), where Allah’s response to human gratitude surpasses the cumulative rewards listed by the angels, culminating in the promise of direct divine mercy.
